title: Network Troubleshooting Toolkit
oneLiner: Six support tickets, each a different fault in a real lab network. Run ip, ping, traceroute, nslookup, curl and ss, read the real output, and name the cause.
keyTakeaway: Troubleshoot bottom up: is the link up and is there an address, can I reach my gateway, can I reach the server's IP, does the name resolve, is the port open, does the application answer? The first layer that fails is where the problem is, and the exact error (timeout or refused, unreachable or no reply) narrows it further.
explanation:
"The network is down" can mean a dozen different things. A fixed order of checks turns guessing into a short process, and it follows the layers from The OSI & TCP/IP Models upward. First the link and address: is the interface up, does it have a sensible address and a default gateway (ip addr and ip route on Linux, ipconfig /all on Windows)? Then the local network: does the gateway answer a ping, and does ip neigh show its MAC address? Then routing: does the server's IP answer, and what path does traceroute show? Then names: does nslookup or dig turn the name into the right address? Finally the service: does curl get a response from the port, and on the server, does ss show something listening?

The wording of each failure is evidence. A timeout means packets vanished: dropped by a firewall, or sent to a route that goes nowhere. "Connection refused" arrives instantly and means the server's machine answered, but nothing listens on that port or a firewall rejected it. "Destination Host Unreachable" reported by your own PC means it couldn't even get an ARP reply from the next hop. "Could not resolve host" or NXDOMAIN (non-existent domain) is DNS. And ping isn't the last word: many firewalls block ICMP, the protocol ping uses, on purpose, so always test the real port too.

Every output below is real, captured from a small lab network built with Linux network namespaces (isolated network stacks on one machine): a PC, a router and a server running a web server and a DNS server. Each ticket broke one thing. Run the tools in whatever order you like, but bottom up is the habit worth building, then name the cause.
